category: VSM microcontroller families, target boards and firmware attachment
description: The processor models that Proteus VSM can execute real firmware on: the Microchip PIC10/12/16/18/24 and dsPIC33 families, Atmel/Microchip AVR and the Arduino boards built on them, 8051/52 derivatives, NXP/ST/TI ARM7 and Cortex-M0/M3/M4 parts, TI MSP430 and Piccolo, and the MicroPython boards (Raspberry Pi Pico, ESP32-S3, Pyboard). Each family is a separately licensed 'Proteus VSM for …' product; entries record the variant lists, the on-chip peripherals that are simulated, the documented model limitations and the debug file formats each toolchain must produce.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for PIC10/12
tools.description: Licensed processor-model set for Microchip's baseline and enhanced-mid-range 6/8-pin parts. Supported variants include PIC10F200/202/204/206, PIC10F220/222, PIC10F320/322 (and LF), PIC12C508A/509A, PIC12C671/672, PIC12CE518/519/673/674, PIC12F508/509/510, PIC12F609/615/629/675/683, PIC12F752/HV752, PIC12F1501, PIC12F1571/1572 and PIC12F1822/1840 (plus LF versions). The models simulate every port pin including weak pull-ups, all timers with watchdog/sleep/wake-up, the ADC with external voltage-reference pins, comparator and voltage reference modules, code/data EEPROM with code protection and persistence, all interrupt modes including interrupt-on-change, and the CWG, CLC, PWM and NCO modules on variants that have them.
tools.usage: Component Mode > P > Keywords 'PIC12F675' > place; Edit Component > Program File = firmware .hex/.cof; Processor Clock Frequency = e.g. 4MHz

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: Intel HEX or (preferably) COF file from the compiler; COF carries the source-level symbols.

parameters.name: Processor Clock Frequency
parameters.description: Clock the model runs at; must match the value the firmware was built for.

tools.example:
1. Place PIC12F683 and an LED on GP0.
2. Build blink.c with XC8 (COF output) in the Source Code tab.
3. Set Program File to the .cof, Clock Frequency 4MHz, press Play and single-step the ISR.
tools.notes: Documented limitations: HFINTOSC as CLC1 input is not supported, and the internal voltage regulator (VREGCON) and BORCON register effects are not modelled. Compilers configured by VSM Studio for this family: Microchip XC8, Hi-Tech PICC, CCS, MPASM. Included in the Microchip 8-bit bundle and Platinum/Enterprise.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for PIC16
tools.description: Processor models for the mid-range and enhanced mid-range PIC16 family: classic parts such as PIC16F84A, PIC16F627A/628A, PIC16F877A, PIC16F887, PIC16F88 and PIC16F690, the 16F7xx/16F9xx LCD parts, and the enhanced 16F1xxx range (16F1503 to 16F1947, 16F1454/1455/1459 USB parts, 16F18854-18857). Simulated peripherals include CCP/ECCP in all modes, Parallel Slave Port, MSSP in SPI and I2C master/slave modes, 10-bit ADC and the extended 12-bit differential ADC, comparators with internal/external references, USART/EUSART, EEPROM, the LCD controller, CLC, PWM, NCO, CWG, Ultra Low Power Wake-Up, DSM, capacitive sensing (CSM), on-chip op-amp (OPA), 5/8-bit DAC, PSMC and COG.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'PIC16F877A' > Program File property; build with XC8 / Hi-Tech / CCS / MPASM through the Source Code tab

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: HEX, COF (Microchip debug format) or the output of the VSM Studio project.

parameters.name: Processor Clock Frequency
parameters.description: Oscillator frequency; internal-oscillator parts derive it from the OSCCON settings in firmware.

tools.example: Place PIC16F887, wire an LM016L to PORTD, attach lcd_demo.cof, run and open Debug > PIC CPU Registers to watch PORTD change as the LCD is written.
tools.notes: Known limitations: the PGC/PGD programming interface and brown-out detection are not modelled; only PCIE, SCIE, SBCDE and BOEN of the newer SSPCON3 I2C features are supported; HFINTOSC as CLC1 input is not supported; the CSM analogue oscillator is not modelled (capacitance on CPSx inputs is ignored).

tools.name: Proteus VSM for PIC18
tools.description: Processor models for the 8-bit PIC18 family, from PIC18F242/252/442/452 and PIC18F2620/4620 through the K20/K22/K50/K80 series (PIC18F45K20, PIC18F46K22, PIC18F25K50, PIC18F26K80), the USB parts (PIC18F2455/2550/4455/4550, PIC18F13K50/14K50, PIC18F24K50/25K50/45K50), the J-series (PIC18F46J13/47J13, 18F6xJ90/8xJ90), the 80-pin PIC18F8722/8620 and the LCD-driver PIC18F6390/8490 parts; release 8.14 added a further 14 PIC18 variants. On top of the PIC16 peripheral set the PIC18 models add the Parallel Master Port, CTMU, REFO reference clock output, RTCC real-time clock/calendar, SR latch, deep sleep with independent watchdog, Peripheral Pin Select, open-drain outputs and the USB module.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'PIC18F4550' > Program File = firmware .cof/.hex; USB parts also need the USB Simulation Support module for host-side enumeration

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: COF/HEX from XC8, C18 or Hi-Tech PIC18.

parameters.name: Processor Clock Frequency
parameters.description: External clock; PLL multipliers are taken from the configuration bits in the firmware image.

tools.example: PIC18F4550 + USBCONN: attach the Microchip CDC demo .cof, run, and the virtual USB device enumerates on the host PC as a COM port.
tools.notes: Documented limitations: the External Memory Interface of PIC18F8X20 parts, power-managed idle modes (SLEEP always enters full sleep), brown-out/HLVD, IESO/FSCM, the CAN/ECAN module, the Streaming Parallel Port and isochronous USB transfers are not modelled. CAN designs must therefore use an external MCP2515/MCP2518FD controller model instead of the on-chip ECAN.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for PIC24
tools.description: 16-bit Microchip models covering the PIC24F 'GA' general-purpose range (PIC24FJ16/32/48/64GA002/004, PIC24FJ64/96/128GA006/008/010, PIC24FJ32/64GA102/104, PIC24FJ64-256GA106/108/110) and the low-power PIC24F KA parts (PIC24F04KA200/201, PIC24F08KA101/102, PIC24F16KA101/102). Use it for 16-bit designs that need the PMP parallel master port, multiple UART/SPI/I2C modules, input capture/output compare and the 10-bit ADC; firmware is built with MPLAB XC16 (or the older C30) and loaded as a COF/ELF file.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'PIC24FJ64GA002' > Program File = .cof from XC16; Clock Frequency per the firmware's oscillator configuration

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: XC16/C30 COF or ELF debug image.

parameters.name: Processor Clock Frequency
parameters.description: Primary oscillator frequency (FRC/PLL settings come from the configuration words).

tools.example: The 'dsPIC33 Data Recorder' Getting Started sample shows the 16-bit workflow: PIC24/dsPIC MCU, I2C memory, SHT15 sensor, XC16 firmware compiled from the Source Code tab.
tools.notes: PIC32 (MIPS) parts are not simulated by Proteus VSM. The PIC24 and dsPIC33 products are bundled together in the Microchip 8/16-bit bundle. See the technical specification for the current limitations list.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for dsPIC33
tools.description: Digital signal controller models for the dsPIC33FJ general-purpose (GP) and motor-control (MC) parts: dsPIC33FJ12GP201/202, dsPIC33FJ32GP202/204, dsPIC33FJ16GP304, dsPIC33FJ12MC201/202, dsPIC33FJ32MC202/204 and dsPIC33FJ16MC304. The models execute the dsPIC DSP instruction set (MAC, barrel shifter, accumulators) so filter and motor-control firmware built with XC16 runs cycle-accurately against the analogue front end and motor models on the schematic.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'dsPIC33FJ32MC204' > Program File = .cof/.elf from XC16; use the MC variants with the motor-control PWM module

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: XC16 COF/ELF with DWARF debug data.

parameters.name: Processor Clock Frequency
parameters.description: Crystal/oscillator input; PLL configured in firmware.

tools.example: dsPIC33FJ32MC204 driving an IR2104 half-bridge and a BLDC motor model: run the motor-control PWM firmware and watch phase currents on the oscilloscope.
tools.notes: Only the dsPIC33FJ 'F' generation listed above is modelled; dsPIC33E/CK and dsPIC30 parts are not in the supported list. Included in the Microchip 8/16-bit bundle.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for AVR
tools.description: Processor models for the classic Atmel (now Microchip) tinyAVR and megaAVR families used in bare-chip designs, for example ATmega8/16/32/48/88/168/328P, ATmega64/128/1280/2560, ATmega32U4 and ATtiny13/25/45/85/2313/24/44/84. The models simulate ports, timers/counters with PWM, USART, SPI, TWI (I2C), the ADC and analogue comparator, EEPROM, watchdog and sleep modes, and load ELF/DWARF or COFF debug images so C code from AVR-GCC can be single-stepped.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'ATMEGA328P' > Program File = .elf/.hex; Clock Frequency = 16MHz (external) or leave fuses to select the internal 8MHz RC

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: ELF/DWARF (AVR-GCC), COFF, AVRASM object or BASCOM .obj.

parameters.name: Processor Clock Frequency
parameters.description: External clock value; CKSEL/CKDIV8 fuse behaviour is taken from the Advanced Properties/fuse settings.

tools.example: ATmega16 + LM016L: compile with WinAVR/AVR-GCC (-g for DWARF), set Program File to main.elf, run and open the Watch Window on PORTC.
tools.notes: XMEGA and the newer AVR-Dx/tinyAVR-1 series are not in the published supported list; check the Pick Devices 'show only parts with models' filter. Toolchains VSM Studio configures: WinAVR/AVR-GCC, AVRASM, BASCOM AVR and the Arduino AVR core. The AVR product also ships as an AVR Starter Kit.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for Arduino AVR
tools.description: Board-level models of the AVR-based Arduino boards - Arduino Uno, Mega, Leonardo, Nano and Yun plus the Seeeduino Cloud - that place a complete board (MCU, headers, USB-serial, regulators) as a single schematic part. Sketches are compiled with the Arduino AVR core toolchain that VSM Studio downloads and configures, and the resulting ELF is attached so the sketch can be single-stepped while shields, Grove modules and breakout boards from the Visual Designer peripheral gallery respond on the schematic.
tools.usage: File > New Project > Firmware: Family 'Arduino', Controller 'Arduino Uno' (Visual Designer or source-code project); or Pick Devices > 'ARDUINO UNO R3'

parameters.name: Controller
parameters.description: Uno, Mega, Leonardo, Nano, Yun or Seeeduino Cloud.

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: Sketch ELF produced by the Arduino AVR core build; set automatically by the Source Code/Visual Designer project.

tools.example: New Project > Visual Designer for Arduino > Arduino Uno > Add Peripheral > Grove LED; build and run - the LED on the Grove module blinks on the schematic.
tools.notes: All Arduino AVR variants are included in the AVR family licence. Shields that use the same CPU resource (e.g. Timer1) conflict, and an Uno can run out of memory with large shield stacks - the Visual Designer help recommends the Mega for those.

tools.name: Arduino Uno (target board model)
tools.description: The most common Visual Designer / VSM target: an ATmega328P-based board model exposing the D0-D13 and A0-A5 header terminals so shields and Grove modules connect by terminal name without drawn wires. Selecting it as the controller in the New Project wizard auto-places the board on the schematic and creates a sketch project with the standard Setup and Loop event blocks.
tools.usage: New Project wizard > Firmware > Family Arduino > Controller Arduino Uno; peripherals attach through Project Tree > Add Peripheral

parameters.name: Interface / Port / Port Speed
parameters.description: Project settings used when uploading to real hardware (e.g. Arduino Uno, COMx, 115200).

parameters.name: Embed Files
parameters.description: Keeps source and debug files inside the .pdsprj container.

tools.example: Uno + Adafruit Motor Shield V1 R3: drag the motor 'run' method into Loop, set a speed variable in Setup, build, and step through the subroutine with F11.
tools.notes: Upload to real hardware uses AVRDUDE through the project's Program Settings; the simulation clock and the real board clock can differ, so set 'Clock For Delays' to the expected hardware value if timing looks wrong.

tools.name: Arduino Mega 2560 (target board model)
tools.description: ATmega2560 board model with the full 54 digital / 16 analogue header set and four hardware UARTs. Choose it when a project stacks several shields or Grove modules, because it has the memory the Uno lacks for large software stacks (TFT + SD, wave shield, GPS) and enough pins to avoid header clashes.
tools.usage: New Project wizard > Controller 'Arduino Mega'; or Pick Devices > 'ARDUINO MEGA2560'

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: Sketch ELF from the Arduino AVR core (set by the project).

tools.example: Mega + Adafruit TFT shield + SD resource: add the bitmap resource to the Project Tree, drag it into Loop (Visual Designer inserts drawBitmap()), build and run.
tools.notes: The Arduino Yun shield can be mounted on an Uno or Mega to make it an IoT Builder target.

tools.name: Arduino Nano and Leonardo (target board models)
tools.description: Compact Arduino board models: the Nano (ATmega328P, breadboard footprint, same pin map as the Uno) and the Leonardo (ATmega32U4 with native USB, so the sketch can enumerate as a USB CDC/HID device when USB Simulation Support is licensed). Both are selectable as the controller of an Arduino firmware project.
tools.usage: New Project wizard > Controller 'Arduino Nano' or 'Arduino Leonardo'

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: Sketch ELF; Leonardo USB descriptors come from the Arduino core.

tools.example: Leonardo keyboard demo: Keyboard.print() in the sketch types into the host PC through the simulated USB connection.
tools.notes: Nano and Uno share firmware; Leonardo sketches use different pin/timer mappings (32U4).

tools.name: Arduino Yun (IoT Builder target)
tools.description: Board model of the Arduino Yun - an ATmega32U4 plus an Atheros AR9331 Linux SoC with Wi-Fi/Ethernet - used as the primary Arduino IoT Builder target. The flowchart firmware runs on the AVR while the web server and the front-panel graphics are deployed to the Atheros side, so the IoT Controller app or a browser on the same network can drive the appliance. The Yun Shield (on an Uno or Mega) and an ESP8266 breakout are the alternative Arduino IoT targets.
tools.usage: New flowchart project > target 'Arduino Yun' (or add the Yun shield / ESP8266 from the Internet of Things peripherals); Project Tree > right-click Yun > Add IoT control

parameters.name: Programmer
parameters.description: YUNSSH (Wi-Fi/Ethernet via SSH, runs AVRDUDE on the Atheros side) or USB.

parameters.name: Port Speed
parameters.description: 57600 by default for the Yun.

tools.example: Blink-an-LED tutorial: place a push button IoT control on the panel, create a button event, drag LED on/off methods into it, run, then press the button in the IoT Controller phone app.
tools.notes: A Yun Shield mounted on an Uno/Mega cannot be programmed over USB because the serial link is in use - program it via SSH. Ethernet/Wi-Fi models were improved in Proteus 9.2.

tools.name: STM32F103C8T6 Blue Pill (STM32 Arduino target)
tools.description: Added in Proteus 8.14: a Cortex-M3 STM32F103C8T6 'Blue Pill' board model that can be programmed from Visual Designer/VSM Studio with the STM32 Arduino core, giving Arduino-style sketches on a 72MHz ARM. It uses the Cortex-M3 processor model (Proteus VSM for ARM Cortex-M3 licence) and accepts the ELF/DWARF file the GCC-based STM32 core produces.
tools.usage: New Project wizard > Family 'STM32 Arduino' > Controller 'Blue Pill'; or Pick Devices > 'STM32F103C8' and attach an ELF built with GCC for ARM/Keil/IAR

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: ELF/DWARF from the STM32 Arduino core, GCC for ARM, Keil MDK or IAR.

tools.example: Blue Pill + SSD1306 OLED (I2C): compile an Adafruit_GFX sketch with the STM32 core, run, and step the I2C writes with the I2C Protocol Analyser attached to PB6/PB7.
tools.notes: Requires the ARM Cortex-M3 (or ARM Bundle) VSM licence in addition to Visual Designer for Arduino.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for 8051/52
tools.description: Processor models for MCS-51 derivatives: generic 80C31/80C32/80C51/80C52/80C54/80C58, Atmel AT89C51/AT89C52/AT89C55 and AT89C51RB2/RC2/RD2, and Philips/NXP P87C51FA/FB/FC and P87C51RA+/RB+/RC+/RD+ (the product is sold as 'Proteus VSM for NXP 8051 variants' and a separate Atmel 8051/52 family). Timers, UART, external memory bus (with the 74HC373 latch and external RAM/ROM models), interrupts and idle/power-down modes are simulated, and the debugger loads Keil OMF51, SDCC CDB or IAR UBROF files for source-level stepping.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'AT89C52' > Program File = .omf (Keil) / .cdb-linked .ihx (SDCC) / .hex; Clock Frequency = 12MHz

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: OMF51 (Keil), CDB (SDCC), UBROF (IAR) or HEX/assembler output from ASEM-51.

parameters.name: Processor Clock Frequency
parameters.description: Crystal frequency; 12 clocks per machine cycle on standard cores.

tools.example: AT89S52 + LM016L in 4-bit mode: build with SDCC (--debug) in the Source Code tab, attach the output, and break on the LCD init routine.
tools.notes: AT89S52 users normally simulate with the AT89C52 model (same core/peripherals). Also available as an 8051 Starter Kit licence. Compilers VSM Studio configures: Keil uVision C51, SDCC, IAR, ASEM-51 (assembler only).

tools.name: Proteus VSM for ARM7/LPC2000
tools.description: Models of NXP's ARM7TDMI-S LPC2000 microcontrollers: LPC2101/2102/2103, LPC2104/2105/2106, LPC2114/2124 and LPC2131/2132/2134/2136/2138, plus bare ARM7TDMI and ARM7TDMI-S core models. Both the ARM and Thumb instruction sets are executed, with all on-chip peripherals (GPIO, timers, RTC, UARTs, SPI, I2C, MAM, PLL, ADC) and the full VIC interrupt controller; throughput is quoted at up to 10 MIPS on a 3GHz PC and any ELF/DWARF2 image can be loaded and debugged.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'LPC2138' > Program File = .elf (GCC for ARM, Keil, IAR); Clock Frequency = crystal (PLL from firmware)

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: ELF/DWARF2 from GCC, Keil uVision or IAR Embedded Workbench.

tools.example: LPC2138 UART0 to a Virtual Terminal at 9600 baud; debugger drivers also allow IAR EW and Keil UV3 to drive the simulation remotely.
tools.notes: Limitations: the bootloader is not modelled and JTAG/in-circuit programming modes are not supported. Consistency checks flag invalid opcodes, illegal memory access and stack overflow in the Simulation Log.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for ARM Cortex-M0/M0+
tools.description: Models for NXP's LPC111x Cortex-M0 range (LPC1110FD20, LPC1111/1112/1113/1114 in FDH20/FHN33/FBD48/FN28 packages and /101 to /333 revisions, LPC1115FBD48/FET48) and Microchip's Cortex-M0+ ATSAMD21E/G/J15A-18A parts. Ports, timers, UART, SPI/SSP, I2C, ADC and the NVIC are simulated and ELF/DWARF images from GCC, Keil or IAR are debugged at source level.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'LPC1114FBD48/302' or 'ATSAMD21G18A' > Program File = .elf

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: ELF/DWARF debug image.

tools.example: ATSAMD21G18A running an Arduino-Zero-style sketch built with GCC for ARM; monitor SERCOM0 UART output on the Virtual Terminal.
tools.notes: Limitations: flash-programming firmware (IAP/ISP) is not supported and the LPC111x CONIO.HYST hysteresis bit is not modelled.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for ARM Cortex-M3
tools.description: Cortex-M3 models for ST STM32F103C4/R4/T4/C6/R6/T6 (the STM32F1 family support was completed in Proteus 8.6 and the STM32F103C8T6 Blue Pill added in 8.14), TI Stellaris LM3S300/301/308/310/315/316/317/328, NXP LPC1311/1313/1342/1343 (FHN33/FBD48) and Atmel ATSAM3N4B. The whole instruction set (except multiprocessor operations) is executed with sleep/deep-sleep, watchdog, general-purpose timers, UART with FIFO, SSI (Freescale, MICROWIRE and TI frame formats), I2C, analogue comparators, a 10-bit ADC with internal temperature sensor and the memory protection unit.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'STM32F103C6' / 'LM3S316' > Program File = .elf from GCC for ARM, Keil MDK or IAR

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: ELF/DWARF from IAR, GCC or Keil (the VSM Studio toolchains for ARM).

tools.example: STM32F103 + ILI9341 TFT over SPI1: build with GCC for ARM, attach main.elf, run, and use the SPI Protocol Analyser to check the command/data sequence.
tools.notes: Limitations: bit-band alias regions are execute-never, cache information and SYST_CALIB are ignored, DMB/DSB act as NOP, PLLCFG, clock-verification timers, brown-out detector, DR2R/DR4R/DR8R/SLR registers and the I2C loopback are not modelled. STM32CubeIDE can debug the simulation over GDB from Proteus 9.2.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for ARM Cortex-M4
tools.description: Cortex-M4 models for the ST STM32F401 (CB/CC/CD/CE, VB/VC/VD/VE, RB/RC/RD/RE) and STM32F407 (IE/IG/ZE/VE/VG/ZG) parts, i.e. the devices on the Nucleo-F401RE and STM32F4 Discovery boards. Peripheral coverage follows the STM32 Cortex-M3 models with the F4 timers, USARTs, SPI/I2C, ADC/DAC and NVIC; firmware is any ELF/DWARF file from GCC for ARM, Keil MDK or IAR.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'STM32F407VG' > Program File = .elf; Clock Frequency = HSE crystal (8MHz), PLL from firmware

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: ELF/DWARF from IAR, GCC or Keil.

tools.example: STM32F407VG blinking PD12-PD15 (Discovery LEDs) from a CubeMX-generated GCC project attached as .elf; debug it from STM32CubeIDE through the Proteus GDB server (9.2).
tools.notes: Only the F401 and F407 series are listed; other STM32F4/F7/G4/H7 parts are not modelled. Included in the ARM Bundle.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for ARM Bundle
tools.description: A single licence covering every ARM family Proteus models - ARM7/LPC2000, Cortex-M0/M0+, Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4 - intended for users who need more than one ARM core (for example STM32F1 and STM32F4 in the same lab). Platinum and Enterprise packages include it by definition.
tools.usage: Purchase 'Proteus VSM for ARM Bundle' in the package configurator; the family then appears in Pick Devices and in the New Project wizard family list
tools.example: Mixed lab pack: LPC2138 boards for one course and STM32F407 boards for another are both simulated under the one bundle key.
tools.notes: Each individual family remains purchasable separately; all ARM models load ELF/DWARF firmware.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for MSP430
tools.description: Models of Texas Instruments' 16-bit MSP430 ultra-low-power microcontrollers (the classic MSP430F/G value-line and 2xx/4xx parts), simulating the RISC core, low-power modes LPM0-4, Timer_A/B, USCI/USART serial modules, ADC10/ADC12 and comparators. Firmware from Code Composer Studio (COFF/DWARF) or GCC for MSP430 is attached for source-level debugging.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'MSP430G2553' > Program File = .out (CCS COFF) or .elf (GCC MSP430); Clock Frequency per DCO/crystal

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: COFF/DWARF from Code Composer or ELF from MSP430-GCC.

tools.example: MSP430 LaunchPad-style circuit: attach blink.out, run, and check that the model enters LPM3 by watching the status-bar simulation time advance between timer interrupts.
tools.notes: Both the Code Composer MSP430 and GCC for MSP430 toolchains are configured by VSM Studio. Consult the TI technical specification document for the exact variant list of your release.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for PICCOLO
tools.description: Models of TI's C2000 Piccolo (TMS320F280xx) 32-bit real-time control MCUs, aimed at digital power and motor-control designs. The C28x core, ePWM/HRPWM, eCAP, eQEP, 12-bit ADC and SCI/SPI/I2C modules run firmware built with Code Composer Studio, so control loops can be tested against the motor, gate-driver and switching-converter models in the peripheral library.
tools.usage: Pick Devices > 'TMS320F28027' (Piccolo) > Program File = Code Composer .out (COFF/DWARF)

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: COFF/DWARF output of Code Composer for PICCOLO.

tools.example: Piccolo driving a buck converter through a gate-driver model; view the ePWM output and inductor current on the oscilloscope while stepping the ADC ISR.
tools.notes: Sold as a separate TI family licence alongside MSP430; included in Platinum/Enterprise.

tools.name: Proteus VSM for MicroPython
tools.description: Launched with Proteus 8.17 SP4 as a separately licensed product, this simulates complete MicroPython systems: the interpreter runs on a Raspberry Pi Pico/Pico W, Arduino Nano ESP32, ESP32-S3-DEVKITC-1 or (from 9.0) Pyboard V1.x board model, with single-step debugging of the Python source, an integrated REPL console for issuing commands and inspecting or modifying variables while the simulation runs, and automatic driver blocks for attached hardware. Proteus 9.1 added Visual Designer for MicroPython (flowchart programming) and IoT Builder for MicroPython.
tools.usage: New Project > Firmware > Family 'MicroPython' > board (Pico W, ESP32-S3, Nano ESP32, Pyboard); edit main.py in the Source Code tab or build a flowchart in Visual Designer

parameters.name: Board
parameters.description: Raspberry Pi Pico, Pico W, Nano ESP32, ESP32-S3-DEVKITC-1 or Pyboard V1.x.

parameters.name: REPL console
parameters.description: Interactive prompt available during simulation for live variable inspection.

tools.example: Pico W + DHT22 + SSD1306: write main.py using machine.Pin/I2C, run, set a breakpoint in the read loop and inspect the humidity value in the REPL.
tools.notes: Requires the VSM for MicroPython licence (not covered by the AVR/ARM keys). Visual Designer and IoT Builder for MicroPython are additional modules; Platinum includes the MicroPython bundle.

tools.name: Raspberry Pi Pico / Pico W (RP2040 MicroPython target)
tools.description: Board models of the RP2040-based Raspberry Pi Pico and the Wi-Fi-equipped Pico W, the launch targets of Proteus VSM for MicroPython. The 40-pin header terminals (GP0-GP28, ADC inputs, I2C/SPI/UART) connect peripheral gallery items and ordinary schematic parts, and the Pico W's wireless link makes it a MicroPython IoT Builder target for MQTT dashboards.
tools.usage: New Project > MicroPython > 'Raspberry Pi Pico W'; program in the Source Code tab (main.py) or Visual Designer for MicroPython

parameters.name: main.py
parameters.description: MicroPython program executed by the on-board interpreter.

tools.example: Pico W reading a Grove temperature sensor and publishing to an IoT Builder gauge over MQTT; single-step the publish call and watch the panel update.
tools.notes: RP2040 is not available as a bare C/C++ (Pico SDK) target - the Proteus support is MicroPython only. The PIO state machines are not documented as modelled.

tools.name: ESP32-S3-DEVKITC-1 and Arduino Nano ESP32 (MicroPython targets)
tools.description: Espressif ESP32-S3 board models supported by Proteus VSM for MicroPython: the ESP32-S3-DEVKITC-1 development kit and the Arduino Nano ESP32. They provide the Xtensa-based interpreter with GPIO, ADC, I2C, SPI, UART and PWM machine modules and the Wi-Fi network object needed for IoT Builder projects, so the same MicroPython script that runs in simulation can be copied to the physical board.
tools.usage: New Project > MicroPython > 'ESP32-S3-DEVKITC-1' or 'Nano ESP32'

parameters.name: main.py
parameters.description: MicroPython program; network.WLAN is available for IoT Builder connectivity.

tools.example: Nano ESP32 + NeoPixel strip: use the neopixel module in main.py, run, and step the write() call while the LED chain animates on the schematic.
tools.notes: ESP32 is not available as an Arduino C++/ESP-IDF target in Proteus; only the MicroPython firmware path is simulated. The original ESP32 (non-S3) is not in the published board list.

tools.name: Pyboard V1.x (MicroPython target)
tools.description: Added in Proteus 9.0: the official MicroPython Pyboard V1.x (STM32F405 based) as a VSM for MicroPython target, giving the pyb module API (pyb.LED, pyb.Switch, pyb.ADC, pyb.Timer) in simulation alongside the machine module.
tools.usage: New Project > MicroPython > 'Pyboard V1.x'

parameters.name: main.py
parameters.description: MicroPython program using pyb/machine modules.

tools.example: pyb.LED(1).toggle() in a timer callback; run and confirm the on-board LED animates at the callback rate.
tools.notes: Included with the MicroPython family licence; no separate ARM licence is needed for the Pyboard's STM32 core.

tools.name: Raspberry Pi 3 / Raspberry Pi 3 with Grove (Visual Designer target)
tools.description: Visual Designer for Raspberry Pi simulates the Pi 3 base board (or 'Raspberry Pi 3 with Grove', the Pi 3 with the GrovePi+ HAT stacked on top) as the target for flowchart or Python programs. HATs from the Adafruit and Pimoroni categories, Grove modules and breakout boards auto-place and auto-connect on the schematic by terminal name, and the finished program deploys to a physical Pi over the network with one click (Proteus talks to the Pi over SSH using the drivers installed on Raspbian).
tools.usage: New Project > Visual Designer for Raspberry Pi > base board 'Raspberry Pi 3' or 'Raspberry Pi 3 with Grove'; Project Tree > Add Peripheral (Adafruit / Pimoroni / Grove / Breakout)

parameters.name: Base board
parameters.description: Raspberry Pi 3 or Raspberry Pi 3 with Grove (GrovePi+).

parameters.name: Program settings
parameters.description: Pi hostname/IP, username and password for deployment.

tools.example: Pi 3 + Adafruit DC and Stepper Motor HAT: drag setSpeed()/run() methods into the loop, simulate, then Program to transfer the Python to the real Pi.
tools.notes: Raspberry Pi Zero W works when 'Pi 3' is selected (identical pinout); Raspberry Pi 2 is not supported because its pinout differs. Pi 4 is not in the published list. The Visual Designer project can be converted to a Python script for hand coding.

tools.name: VSM family bundles and Starter Kits (licensing)
tools.description: How processor support is licensed. Each family is a 'Proteus VSM for …' product; Microchip parts are also sold as the PIC 8-bit bundle (PIC10/12/16/18), the PIC 8/16-bit bundle (adds PIC24 and dsPIC33) and a PIC Starter Kit; AVR (with Arduino) and 8051 have Starter Kit editions; ARM has the ARM Bundle; TI covers MSP430 and Piccolo; MicroPython is its own family. Platinum includes every family (over 750 processor models) and Enterprise includes all MCU families for commercial PCB design.
tools.usage: Pricing > Package Configurator > 'Circuit Simulation' > choose the VSM family products, or buy Platinum/Enterprise
tools.example: A university teaching PIC16 and Arduino buys 'PIC 8-bit bundle' + 'AVR (with Arduino)'; a research group needing STM32F4 adds 'ARM Cortex-M4'.
tools.notes: Parts from an unlicensed family still appear in Pick Devices but will not simulate. Starter Kits are the entry-level, capacity-limited editions.

tools.name: Processor Clock Frequency property
tools.description: The Edit Component field on every microcontroller model that sets the simulated oscillator frequency. Cycle timing, baud-rate generation, timer periods and delay loops all derive from it, so it must equal the clock the firmware was compiled for (F_CPU, _XTAL_FREQ, SystemCoreClock); a mismatch shows up as wrong UART baud rates or LCD timing failures.
tools.usage: Double-click the MCU > Processor Clock Frequency = 16MHz (SI suffixes accepted: 4MHz, 32.768kHz)

parameters.name: Value
parameters.description: Frequency with SI suffix; for internal-oscillator parts it is the external input only and the internal RC is configured by the firmware's fuse/OSCCON settings.

tools.example: PIC16F877A firmware built with _XTAL_FREQ 20000000 > set Processor Clock Frequency = 20MHz; with 4MHz the 9600-baud UART output appears as garbage on the Virtual Terminal.
tools.notes: The crystal drawn on the schematic is not used by the processor model for timing - only this property is. Visual Designer additionally offers a 'Clock For Delays' value used when the real board clock differs from the simulation clock.

tools.name: Advanced Properties (microcontroller model options)
tools.description: The lower section of an MCU's Edit Component dialogue that exposes model-specific options chosen from a combo box, such as randomising program/data memory at start-up, watchdog-timer behaviour, initial EEPROM contents, fuse/configuration overrides on AVR parts and per-model diagnostic switches. They tune how faithfully the model mimics power-up conditions and allow the debugger to trap uninitialised-memory bugs.
tools.usage: Edit Component > 'Advanced Properties' combo > select an item > set its value in the field beside it

parameters.name: Randomize Program/Data Memory
parameters.description: Fill unprogrammed memory with random data so code that relies on zeroed RAM fails visibly.

parameters.name: Fuse / configuration bits
parameters.description: AVR CKSEL/CKDIV8/WDTON style options where the firmware image does not carry them.

tools.example: AVR project runs at 1MHz instead of 8MHz: open Advanced Properties and clear the CKDIV8 fuse option (or set Clock Frequency to match the fuse-divided value).
tools.notes: The available items differ per family; PIC configuration words are normally taken from the firmware image itself (__CONFIG / #pragma config). Check the current entries in your release's dialogue.

tools.name: Debug file formats (COF, ELF/DWARF, UBROF, OMF51, CDB, OBJ, BAS)
tools.description: The object formats each processor family accepts in the Program File property when source-level debugging is wanted instead of a bare HEX: PIC uses Microchip COF (any C compiler, MPASM) and Proton BASIC .BAS; AVR uses ELF/DWARF or COFF, BASCOM AVR .OBJ and AVRASM output; 8051 uses Keil OMF51, SDCC CDB and IAR UBROF; ARM Cortex-M and ARM7 use ELF with DWARF; MSP430 and Piccolo use Code Composer COFF/DWARF. A plain .HEX executes correctly on every family but gives no source, variable or breakpoint-by-line support.
tools.usage: Edit Component > Program File = path to the debug file; VSM Studio sets it automatically after a build

parameters.name: Compiler debug switch
parameters.description: e.g. -g for GCC (DWARF), 'Debug' build configuration in XC8 (COF), --debug for SDCC (CDB).

tools.example: Building an STM32 project in Keil with 'Create ELF/DWARF' enabled and attaching project.axf/.elf lets you set breakpoints in main.c inside the Source Code tab.
tools.notes: If a variable shows the wrong value after a rebuild, its address moved - remove and re-add it to the Watch Window. Formats are listed per family on the compilers page.

tools.name: Development board projects (New Project Wizard)
tools.description: The New Project wizard's 'development board' option imports a pre-drawn schematic of a real evaluation board together with the vendor's demonstration source code, so a simulation and a matching VSM Studio project exist immediately. The Getting Started guide uses the Microchip F1 Evaluation Board (PIC16F1937, 'F1 Release') this way, and Arduino base boards are created the same way from the Firmware page of the wizard.
tools.usage: Home page > New Project > choose the development board option > microcontroller family (e.g. PIC16) > board (e.g. F1 Evaluation Board) > Finish

parameters.name: Family
parameters.description: Filters the board list (PIC16, PIC18, Arduino, ...).

parameters.name: Board
parameters.description: Pre-drawn schematic + firmware project template.

tools.example: New Project > development board > PIC16 > 'F1 Evaluation board (F1 Release)' > Finish: two tabs open, the schematic and VSM Studio holding Microchip's demo code ready to Build.
tools.notes: The imported firmware may need a specific compiler (the F1 demo needs Hi-Tech PICC 9.8+); use Compilers Configuration > Check All after installing it.

tools.name: USB Simulation Support
tools.description: The add-on module that lets USB-capable processor models (PIC18F2455/2550/4455/4550, PIC18F14K50/25K50/45K50, PIC24FJ GB parts, ATmega32U4/Leonardo) enumerate on the host PC through a virtual USB connection, so CDC serial, HID and mass-storage firmware can be tested against real host drivers. Proteus 9.2 improved the wired USB modelling and added the FT232 USB-serial bridge model for boards that use an external converter.
tools.usage: Place the USB connector part on the schematic wired to the MCU's D+/D- pins, attach the USB firmware, run; the device appears in the host's Device Manager

parameters.name: Connector
parameters.description: USB connector model (USBCONN) linking the simulated bus to the host stack.

tools.example: PIC18F4550 CDC demo: after Play, Windows enumerates a new COM port which a terminal program on the PC can open to talk to the simulated firmware.
tools.notes: Listed as 'USB Simulation Support' in the Platinum/Enterprise contents; isochronous transfers and the PIC18 Streaming Parallel Port are not modelled. Requires installation of the Proteus USB host driver.

tools.name: Per-family model limitations (reference)
tools.description: Labcenter publishes a 'Limitations' list per processor family in the technical specification documents; the recurring items are: programming interfaces (PGC/PGD, JTAG, ISP bootloaders) are not modelled; brown-out detection, HLVD and internal voltage regulators are not modelled; PIC18 ECAN, external memory interface and power-managed idle modes are not modelled; Cortex-M3 bit-band regions are execute-never and DMB/DSB are NOPs; some clock-verification and calibration registers are ignored. Checking the list before debugging avoids chasing 'bugs' that are simulator omissions.
tools.usage: Read the family's Technical Specifications PDF (labcenter.com/documents) > 'Limitations' section; watch the Simulation Log for 'not modelled' warnings
tools.example: Firmware that waits for the BOR flag after power-up hangs in simulation because brown-out is not modelled on PIC16/18 - guard the wait with a simulation-only #ifdef.
tools.notes: Unmodelled register writes are usually logged as warnings by the Diagnostic Control System; enable the relevant diagnostics for the CPU to see them.

tools.name: Remote debug over GDB (STM32CubeIDE integration)
tools.description: Proteus 9.2 added a GDB Remote Serial Protocol server so IDEs that speak GDB - STM32CubeIDE in particular - can attach to the running Proteus simulation as if it were a hardware probe: breakpoints, stepping and variable inspection happen in the IDE while the circuit, instruments and peripheral models respond in Proteus. It complements the older MPLAB X, Atmel Studio and Keil uVision remote-debug drivers.
tools.usage: Proteus: Debug > Use Remote Debug Monitor (GDB server); STM32CubeIDE: Debug Configuration > 'GDB Hardware Debugging' > connect to the Proteus host/port

parameters.name: Host / port
parameters.description: Address the GDB server listens on (local machine by default).

tools.example: Build the CubeMX project in STM32CubeIDE, start a GDB hardware-debug session pointed at Proteus, and hit a breakpoint in HAL_GPIO_TogglePin while the LED on the schematic freezes mid-toggle.
tools.notes: The ELF must still be attached to the STM32 model's Program File. Available for the ARM Cortex-M models; check the release notes for the current IDE list.
